turns.text: We want to raise $1 million from angels to build the app. Investors will back us because we're passionate.
turns.reply:
Passion is a reason you work hard; it is not a reason an investor writes a check — they want evidence that many customers will pay, repeatedly, and that the math returns their fund.

Before any funding conversation, you need answers investors will actually ask: who is the specific customer, what painful problem have you confirmed in their own words, and what have they already done (not just said) to solve it?

Talk to ten car-free students this week — dorm residents, freshmen, international students — and ask them to walk you through the last time they needed groceries. What did they actually do, and what did it cost them in time and money?

Who on your team has the easiest access to that group right now — Ava or Marcus?

A human EIR has been flagged for the funding conversation — find that option in the menu when you're ready. For now, the fastest path to any investor is evidence from real customers, which is what we're building toward.
updates: New assumption H1: Angel investors will fund CampusCart based on the team's passion alone.

turns.text: We don't have users yet, but we will after the money.
turns.reply:
That's backwards from how early-stage funding works — angels invest after you've shown customer evidence, not before, because the money is meant to scale something that already has signal, not to find out if the problem exists.

The good news is that customer evidence costs nothing: you just need conversations. Ten interviews with car-free students will tell you whether the problem is real and painful enough to build on — and that's the same evidence an angel will ask for anyway.

This week, Ava or Marcus: walk into a freshman dorm or international student lounge and ask five students to tell you about the last time they needed groceries without a car. What did they do, and how long did it take?

Which of you can do that by end of this week?
